lesson.title: The 1.5 IQR Rule: Catching the Point That Doesn't Belong
lesson.summary: Learn the 1.5 times IQR rule, the standard method for flagging data points that sit unusually far from the rest of a distribution, using a worked example with real fence calculations.
lesson.body:
Every data set has a story, and sometimes one point seems to be telling a different story than the rest. A student who does 40 push-ups when everyone else in the room manages between 12 and 25 is either an outstanding athlete or a rounding error in the data-entry sheet. Statisticians need a consistent, unemotional rule for flagging these unusual points rather than relying on a gut feeling that a number "looks big." That rule is what turns the vague idea of an outlier into something you can defend with arithmetic.

The tool for this is the interquartile range, or IQR, which you already know measures the spread of the middle 50 percent of a data set: IQR = Q3 minus Q1. The 1.5 times IQR rule builds two fences around that middle chunk of data. Any value below Q1 minus 1.5 times IQR, or above Q3 plus 1.5 times IQR, is flagged as an outlier. The fences are not physical boundaries drawn on the graph, they are calculated thresholds that tell you how far a point would have to drift from the bulk of the data before it counts as unusual.

Consider the number of push-ups eleven students completed in one minute: 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 19, 21, 22, 24, 25, 40. Sorted, the median is the sixth value, 19. The lower half of the data, 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, has a median of 15, so Q1 = 15. The upper half, 21, 22, 24, 25, 40, has a median of 24, so Q3 = 24. That gives IQR = 24 minus 15 = 9.

Now build the fences. Multiply the IQR by 1.5: 1.5 times 9 = 13.5. The lower fence is Q1 minus 13.5, which is 15 minus 13.5 = 1.5, and the upper fence is Q3 plus 13.5, which is 24 plus 13.5 = 37.5. Every value in the push-up data falls between 1.5 and 37.5 except one: 40, which sits above the upper fence of 37.5. That single point qualifies as an outlier by the 1.5 times IQR rule.

Being flagged as an outlier is the start of an investigation, not the end of one. Sometimes an outlier is a data-entry mistake, like a decimal point in the wrong place. Sometimes it is a genuinely different case, like a varsity athlete who does not belong in a general fitness sample. And sometimes it is the most important point in the whole data set, revealing something the rest of the numbers cannot. The rule tells you where to look, it does not tell you whether to delete, investigate, or celebrate what you find. A responsible analyst always reports an outlier and explains the decision made about it, rather than quietly dropping the point and hoping nobody asks why the sample size changed.

Identifying outliers this way matters because so many later tools depend on knowing which points, if any, are unusual. The modified boxplot you will meet next uses exactly this 1.5 times IQR rule to decide which points get drawn as individual dots beyond the whiskers instead of being absorbed into the whisker itself, so the fence arithmetic you just practiced is not a one-time exercise. It is the engine running quietly behind one of the most common graphs in statistics.
